speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, November 19, 1982 consideration of the motion of Mr. Gray that Bill C-96, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order. I would just like to mention that there is an agreement among the House Leaders to deal with all stages of this Bill today. Therefore, the motion should be amended and the reference be to send the Bill to the Committee of the Whole, not to the Standing Committee. I want to put on record that all the necessary consent should be sought in due time, but it will be given to allow this Bill to get through all stages today.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. 1 would like to ask the House Leader for some clarification in connection with the procedure that he is now proposing. Is he suggesting that, as a result of a meeting between himself and two Party House Leaders, the procedure can now be changed without putting the matter before the House for unanimous consent? Or are we proceeding as the Orders of the Day state so that I might have a chance to speak on the Bill if I wish to do so? 1 would like to have the House Leader clarify these points 1 have put before the House.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the consent is only to allow the Bill to be dealt with through all stages today. There is no doubt that if the Hon. Member seeks the floor and the Speaker wants to recognize him, he will be allowed to speak during the next few hours available for debate. Debate is not limited to one speaker per Party.

Mr. Speaker, we have agreed to put the Bill through all stages today. If we are to do so, I think the Bill should be in Committee of the Whole before one o'clock. I would think we could have something like two speeches, if the Hon. Member for Edmonton East wants to take his 20 minutes. I would certainly appreciate a few minutes at second reading before we go to Committee of the Whole.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the agreement we made was not specific as to how long debate would last at second reading and in Committee of the Whole. I think we should let debate go on and we shall see what happens later. There was no firm deal as to the number of speakers at second reading, for example.

Mr. Speaker, 1 was somewhat troubled in getting ready for the debate today. There are a substantial number of amendments to this Bill that we have to get through in Committee of the Whole. Was there a breakdown in the proceedings? Why were the amendments not published in the Order Paper? How are we going to handle this? Are they going to be read into the record? Are they going to be handled one at a time as we proceed in Committee of the Whole?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while debate is going on at second reading, we might consider a reasonable approach to dealing with the numerous amendments when we reach Committee of the Whole stage. I will speak with the President of the Treasury Board. I have a meeting with the House Leaders in 15 minutes. If we can be useful, fine. The agreement was that we dispose of the Bill today in the House of Commons. If we have the time to deal with all the amendments, fine. If we do not have the time, they will have to be voted on very quickly.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government House Leader sets forth with accuracy the fact that there has been agreement to pass the Bill through all three stages today which, of course, does not prevent the Hon. Member for Edmonton East from speaking. I was unaware of any Government amendments with respect to the legislation and presumably there are such amendments. It might facilitate the matter and would certainly be a courtesy to all Members of the House if we could have copies of those amendments distributed to all Hon. Members. This has caught me somewhat by surprise.
Another thing I should say is that I agree with the Hon. Member for Capilano. We should try to move on to Committee of the Whole to deal with these amendments as quickly as possible and I think that that could be accomplished if we were to hold the number of speakers down to a minimum on second reading.
If I might have the attention of the Government House Leader so that he can concur, the third thing I would like to remind him of is that we agreed to deal with this Bill today. If it happens to conclude before six o'clock today, we will see the clock as being six o'clock with no intervening business after the conclusion of this business and before the six o'clock closing of business.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

November 24, 1983
Financial Administration Act

Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same point of order. 1 am not sure that I have full clarification in my mind as to what is going on in the House at this particular moment. The Government House Leader indicated that an agreement has been reached to make certain that the Bill passes today. 1 recognize that I sit as an independent and can only speak once on second reading and once on third reading, 1 hope.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: But you are unlimited in Committee of the Whole.

I know that. I can speak during Committee of the Whole in terms of the number of amendments that are made, and indeed they are quite substantive. If a person were to get really interested in asking questions about these amendments, I imagine he could hold the Bill up for several hours and indeed for several days.
My point of view again, Mr. Speaker, is not that I am particularly interested in the Bill. I am interested in the procedure which goes on in the House with respect to independents who may be here in the future. There may be 20 of us in the future, I do not know. I am concerned that an agreement has been reached between the three Parties indicating that the Bill should be passed today without putting the matter by way of a vote of unanimous consent in the House. If the matter were to be put and indeed unanimous consent were to be requested, I would be prepared to give that unanimous consent without too much difficulty. However, the point I make is, how can an agreement be made in such a way that it impinges upon my rights in the House without my being party to that agreement?
As I said, if I wished to become miserable, I could certainly delay this Bill beyond the course of the day, particularly in Committee of the Whole. I simply ask again for clarification from the Government House Leader as to whether a request for unanimous consent to this agreement should be put in the House or whether he is simply prepared to go ahead, hoping that it will indeed pass in the course of the day if I do not become too mouthy, if you wish, in terms of asking questions in Committee of the Whole.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: He was asking for consent.

If he is asking for consent, then I expect the Speaker will put the request for unanimous consent to deal with the Bill in its entirety this day to the House. If the Speaker does so, then I would certainly be prepared to give my consent.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if you seek that consent, we are prepared to give that consent as well.

Member, I am prepared to do that as well. I will recognize whoever rises. The Hon. Member for Capilano.
November 24, 1983

Mr. Speaker, I am glad that we have got through the initial procedural problem. It will not be an easy day. Just as we came into the House we were given this package of amendments which we will have to deal with through the Committee of the Whole stage. Since they are not printed in our Order Paper, I understand we will have to read them into the record.
In this Bill we are dealing with amendments to the Financial Administration Act. The call and demand for these amendments has come out of a long series of meetings and many hours of deliberation between the Auditor General and his staff, the Standing Committee on Public Accounts and the Treasury Board. These are housekeeping amendments which are probably meant to bring us out of the quill pen age, as the Comptroller General says, and up to the computer age. They are highly technical.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Lang) was good enough to meet with me as the Official Opposition critic of the Treasury Board and we spent some hours on these. I have been assured by the Comptroller General that each of these amendments is necessary. I just want to explain that the reason for all of these amendments is to take care of objections that the Office of the Auditor General has had to Bill C-96 in its printed form. These amendments have come a long way toward doing that.
At the outset, I must say that one of the matters that was not agreeable to us during the negotiation stage was Clause 3. We had problems dealing with that clause. The wording was submitted to me by the Comptroller General. I would assume that the wording as submitted to me by him, amending Clause 3 to fit with anxieties that we had, is what is in this package. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) nods yes. So that concern is covered.
Over the years, I suppose since Auditor General Macdonell flew the signal in March of 1976 that spending was out of control, a hard working group, including the Deputy Speaker, has worked on procedures and attitudes to try and bring the matter back under control. I stand here as a person who is very concerned at what has happened to our Government and what is going to happen to our country if somehow or other Hon. Members in this House cannot deliver themselves to a new direction and to a new attitude-and it is going to have to be an apolitical attitude-in order to bring the runaway, out of control spending of the Government of Canada under control. It is not necessarily totally the fault of the incumbent Government, but it has to accept the responsibility for what has happened to the country in the last 14 years. The matter is of crisis proportion today.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), on August 13, 1969, recognized that the behaviour of governments in Canada and in the western world was going to cause serious deprivation and problems for the poor, the sick and the elderly. I stand here to make a plea to all Members of this House of Commons, my own Party, the New Democratic Party, the Government Party and the independent, that if we are going to bring the system under control, we are going to have to change our
Financial Administration Act
attitudes. We in this House, as individual Members, are to blame. We are the politicians. We go to the electorate and make promises and we are proud of what we deliver back into our constituencies. There are Hon. Members who are proud of what they can gather here and deliver back. That seems to be how the people of Canada relate to politicians. They seem to accept half-truths.
I am suggesting to you, Sir, that we are at the end of that road. What we are dealing with in this Bill is just the beginning. All we are doing is dealing with the technical aspects of the Financial Administration Act, to allow for some of the new value for money concepts which we passed in our Auditor General Act and in the amendments to the Financial Administration Act which gave us the Comptroller General and will allow the central agency of the Treasury Board and the office of the Comptroller General to function and overcome the handicaps, abuses and voids which the Auditor General has been pointing out for some years now.
I do not have trouble in agreeing to the Bill. Our Party is going to support the Bill in order to get it through the House all in one day. However, I would want each element of it to be talked about and understood. It is good for Members of this House to have an understanding of what we are doing.
I rise to take time on second reading to make an appeal. We, as a western world nation, are in a catch-22 situation. I have just come from the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, which was questioning the Secretary of the Treasury Board. I can appreciate that the President of the Treasury Board has been busy getting ready for this day in the House, but it is unfortunate that he was not in that Committee this morning because the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates is a Committee of the House dealing with policy. We examine senior Deputy Ministers, like the Secretary of the Treasury Board in the Standing Committee on Public Accounts; and in that standing committee we are apolitical and do not touch policy. However, with the nation in the dilemma in which it is today, in spite of the Prime Minister's warning back in 1969, the whole system is out of control. In spite of the Auditor General's warning in March of 1976, we are in 1983 even further out of control and something has to be done. We have to cross Party lines and cross the bridge between the politicians and the professionals who manage the federal Government system.
In my opinion and that of many others, if we continue this way the system will go into total collapse. Those social policies we are so proud of in Canada are going to collapse with it. Our pensions are going to collapse. We cannot get this country back on its feet creating wealth if we have a fat, careless, slothful overburden in the form of government. We can trim the federal Government, make it lean and effective, as our value for money legislation calls for. But I really fear for the people of Canada if we continue the way we are because we

November 24, 1983
Financial Administration Act
are harming those who cannot look after themselves, those who are about to rely on their pensions for a modest standard of living in the twilight years of their life. It is not just Canada, Mr. Speaker. Other nations have tried, too-deliberately and too energetically, to redistribute wealth. 1 suggest we have gone so far in that direction that we have smothered the creation of wealth.
What we are dealing with today is a technical move which should remove a lot of the excuses the central agency gives for not being able to control the system. Guideline after guideline and regulation after regulation in the central agency are so permissive you can drive trucks through them. I plead for this House to accept responsibility for financial management and make sure tax dollars are used wisely, efficiently and effectively. But it 'aint going to happen, Sir, unless we as individual Members in this House do it.
I have to compliment most of the people in the federal bureaucracy, Mr. Speaker. The Comptroller General has put in place all the things we asked him to do. He asked for five years and that is coming forward. The new form of the Estimates is coming down and the President of the Treasury Board has requested Members to comment on the new Part I Is. All of this reorganization and proper disclosure of information we hope will allow us to overcome the extravagance we see within Government today. I put a lot of faith in the new form of Estimates and proper disclosure of honest information to hold the system to better account. But none of that is going to happen, none of the work of the federal bureaucracy will come to fruition-and I guess we have spent close to $200 million on this since I was Chairman of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts-unless the individual Member who sits in this House representing the Canadian taxpayer changes his attitude and starts to conserve the tax resources of Canada.
The taxes paid by working people represent blood, sweat and tears. They spend the best part of their day earning their wages from which taxes are deducted. Corporations in Canada add to the value of goods. If they do not do it efficiently and effectively, they are not around for very long in this competitive world.
The energy, skill, the thought and the engineering, the professionalism which goes into creating the profits from which we draw taxes, are held in disrepute and disrespect here. Some 65 per cent of Canadians say this place is no longer relevant and they are right. This is taxation without representation. We have a Department of National Revenue which can walk right into an individual's bank account without even asking the person concerned and take money through some kind of power they have developed with the banks. There is fear among the people of this nation that the arbitrary powers of Government are out of control.
It is up to us, Mr. Speaker. If we want to continue to conduct ourselves in the historical pattern of politicians, then I suggest to every Member sitting in this Chamber that democracy is threatened and will die. It is that serious. Let me just read the concern of the Prime Minister back on August 13, 1969. He said:
This year the debate about inflation and the search for ways to combat it have reached a new intensity. Most Canadians-whether in government, business or labour-realize that if inflation continues unchecked they will suffer personally. But some people suffer more than others. Even a modest increase in general price levels causes anguish for pensioners, wage earners with weak bargaining powers, the unemployed, persons on welfare and other who are unable to increase their incomes. Because these persons are often our lowest income earners inflation has serious implications for our goal of achieving an equitable distribution of incomes.
We have chosen an approach to combat inflation which we believe can produce better long-term results for the country and for Canadians. For success, it requires your support, and this is why 1 am speaking to you tonight.
Our fiscal and monetary policies are the first line of attack. During the past year we have taken necessary steps to place our budget in a surplus position in the 1969-70 fiscal year ... the first actual surplus in thirteen years. This swing from a deficit of $575 million last fiscal year to a surplus this year is of great help in fighting inflation in our economy.
Another important step in holding down costs of all governments in Canada was our refusal to turn over larger amounts of money to the provinces. The Federal stand, and the fruitful discussions held with the provinces before they brought in their budgets, has resulted in most provinces making successful efforts to improve or maintain budgetary balance. I hope they keep up the effort.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and myself were in the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates this morning. One of the problems we were asking about was the increase in the transfer payments to the Provinces, out of control spending and the inability of the central agency, the Treasury Board, to show any semblance of control. I happen to know that the Secretary of the Treasury Board is concerned with the looseness which exists within the system, but we politicians-and I am going to disregard political boundaries-of all stripes are the guilty ones. We do not represent our constituents in matters of supply.
Parliament came about because the King bled the people dry through taxes. That is what the Government is doing in this country and I stand here and say: Enough! Let Bill C-96 be the beginning today of a tightening up of our spending and a representation once again of the taxpayer by Members sitting in this House. If we do not do it I do not know how we are going to survive because we have smothered out the wealth-creating abilities of our land. We cannot see a way to compete with the industries that we have been generous enough to complete in the Third World.
With those remarks, Mr. Speaker, I am going to sit down so that we have maximum time in Committee of the Whole to get through all the amendments we have to deal with.

Mr. Speaker, it was only one hour ago that I became aware that we were going to debate second reading of Bill C-96. I must admit to the House that I have not had the opportunity to prepare a speech. However, I would like to indicate that almost five years ago when I was elected to this Parliament there were three major problems on my mind that, in my view, had a crisis element to them. The first was the patriation of the Constitution and an amending procedure. The second was the reform of Parliamentary institutions. The third was coming to grips with the growth of Governments in Canada, not only provincial and municipal Governments, but the federal Government.
November 24, 1983

Mr. Speaker, 1 spent many hours preparing the first speech that 1 made in this House on October 1 1, 1979. 1 would like to quote a couple of paragraphs from it because 1 dealt with this very matter. I said then:
A recent analysis shows the growth of governments in the free nations of the world in the 20-year period from 1955 to 1975. I will not run through all of them, but I should like to refer to a few examples. In the Netherlands the government's share of the gross national product in 20 years grew from 31.5 per cent to 54 per cent; in Sweden from 16.5 per cent to 52 per cent in 20 years; in Ireland from 28 per cent to 50 per cent; in the United Kingdom from 32.5 per cent to 45 per cent; in Germany from 30 per cent to 44 per cent; in Italy form 28 per cent to 43 per cent; in France from 33 per cent to 42 per cent;-
Over the 20-year period the Government of Canada's share grew from 25 per cent of the GNP to 40 per cent of the GNP. In 1979 the best figures I had indicated that Governments redistributed 42 per cent of the GNP of the nation. At that time I was asked what it was for the United States. I indicated that in the United States it grew from 26 per cent to 36 per cent. 1 also gave figures for some other nations.
That 42 per cent five years ago has now grown, in my view, Mr. Speaker, to 50 per cent of the GNP in Canada. The figures that I have before me are estimates, but the indication is that this year the three levels of Government in Canada will be taking, by way of taxation, 50 per cent of the GNP of this nation for redistribution. In this nation we now have a process where Government redistribution through the taxation system is crushing the ability of the nation to create new wealth.
If there is a problem that has to be faced in every way by every level of Government in Canada, it is to come to grips with this single most important matter in the nation. Creation of wealth must be stimulated again and can only be stimulated by reducing the take from the entrepreneurial and wealth-creating sector of the economy. If there is a point to be made in this House, it is this very point.
I am not going to dwell upon the amendments in this Bill and the additional technical amendments to it in terms of control, but they are hardly enough. I suggest very strongly that at the earliest opportunity the Government of the day should put forth a joint committee of this place and the Senate to examine this area in detail and to come forth with some concrete directions in terms of the control of the growth of Governments in Canada. The federal Government does control, to a large degree, the growth of the provincial Governments through its transfer arrangements, so there is some degree of control from here over the provincial Governments and even over the municipal Governments.
1 appeared before the Joint Committee on Senate Reform and I tried to present a very strong case that the Senate should have the power to review the expenditures of Crown corporations and to limit some of the appropriations to the Crown corporations across this land. That way there would be a check, not only on this place but on the self-perpetuation and growth of Crown corporations themselves. I know how busy Ministers are. They cannot possibly review what goes on within some of these Crown corporations on a daily basis. If commitments are made in these Crown corporations, Ministers
Financial Administration Act
then have to accord with them. Therefore, they have to be stopped in advance rather than after the fact.
I have a Bill on the Order Paper to provide that an Act should be structured to grant Parliament the authority to place Members of parliament and Senators on the board of directors of federal Crown corporations. I received information suggesting that this is not possible because of conflicts of interest and many other reasons. As a Minister in Alberta I put elected members on Crown corporation boards and they were the watchdogs of those Crown corporations. Those elected members functioned extremely well. They put a lot of pressure on the Minister responsible to limit allocations to those Crown corporations and to see that they functioned properly. There was a second line of elected defence by putting an elected member, or in this case a Senator, on some of those Crown corporations at the board level to take note of the decisions that are made at the policy level in these Crown corporations which commit expenditures which can hardly be decreased in this House.
Speaking briefly in a general way to this Bill which deals with the regulation and control of the growth of Governments and expenditures, I am attempting to say that I do not believe for one minute that the mechanism has been found in this Bill to control the growth of government in general and to control the expenditure of the vast complexity of the federal Government. A new system must be found. I hope that the House will either set up joint committee of the House and the Senate to examine all aspects over a period of a year or two of this area of concern for the Parliament of Canada, or devise some better method than I can think of to deal with this most complex and difficult problem within the nation. Because of the very nature of the growth of technology today, expenditures and governments grow irrespective of the dictates of the political process itself.
Mr. Speaker, I want to close by thanking you for the opportunity to make a few remarks on this most important matter. I hope Members of this House will put some points forward regarding a new process for control of the growth and expenditures of government.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments based on some of the things that have been said in the last little while by the Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) and the Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko). No Member of Parliament could disagree with their statements that governments, federal, provincial and municipal, are large organizations and that they have grown larger in recent years. Nobody would disagree with them when they call for efficiency in government.
In the last few years this country, in fact every country in the western industrialized world, has experienced economic recession. It has been obvious that many large organizations, not just public organizations but private organizations, some of them the biggest companies, in the easy years of economic growth and profitability were not as efficient as they could

November 24, 1983
Financial Administration Act
have been. We have seen examples of that. We have examples given to us by the Auditor General and the Comptroller General of mistakes and inefficiencies in government operations. We have seen some very glaring examples in some of our Crown corporations which have obviously not operated very efficiently. 1 refer for example to Canadair. Some problems were not caused by inefficiency but by mistakes in planning because of inability by the corporation concerned and the inability of others to foresee the recession. But it must be pretty obvious to Members of Parliament in the case of Canadair that if one cannot say it was inefficient, it is pretty obvious that it was slow to report its difficulties to the Government; and if Canadair did report its difficulties to the Government and asked for advice, it certainly did not report those difficulties to Parliament.
I join with Members who have spoken, the Hon. Member for Capilano and the Member from Calgary, in supporting the idea that we have to have greater efficiency and that the Government's organization needs to be changed and tightened up so that we get greater efficiency. Where I have some difficulty in following the arguments put forward by the Hon. Member for Capilano and the Member from Calgary is in their sweeping statements about government programs, that we are doing too much, that government is taking too much of the Gross National Product, that we should reduce the percentage of the Gross National Product which goes to government. Governments tax and collect revenue in the way they do, not just for the sake of taxing or for the sake of collecting revenue. Governments spend money to provide services for people, the services which people as individuals, or companies which are in business, cannot provide for themselves.
It was suggested by both Members that we should somehow reduce the transfer payments which are made to the Provinces. I think it is incumbent upon those Members of Parliament or anybody else who believes that government expenditures should be reduced, who believe that the transfer payments made by the federal Government to the provinces should be reduced, to say so. I suggest it is incumbent upon them, if they are serious and believe what they are saying and are going to be honest with other Members of Parliament and with the people of Canada, to indicate much more clearly and much more specifically than they have done today or at any other time just how transfer payments can and should be reduced.
Let us look at some of the reasons the federal Government makes transfer payments. The federal Government has paid over the years approximately 50 per cent of the cost of medicare. Are there Members here who believe we should reduce our expenditures on medicare? If so, they should say so. We have paid approximately 50 per cent of the cost of hospital services. In fact, for some of the poor Provinces like those in Atlantic Canada we have paid more than 50 per cent. Are there Members of Parliament who believe that the federal Government should reduce its share of hospital payments? If so, they should say so. Although we have changed the formula in the legislation and we have changed how we pay for it, over the years we have paid about 50 per cent of the cost of
post-secondary education, the cost of providing university education for those Canadians who want to attend universities and those who want to attend community colleges. Are we doing too much? Are we training too many people in our universities and community colleges? Is it costing us too much? Can we afford it? If Members of Parliament feel that way, I believe it is incumbent upon them to say so and to tell the people.
The federal Government pays for more than 50 per cent of the cost of scientific research in this country. Canada is spending a smaller percentage of its Gross National Product on scientific research than any other country in the industrialized world. The stated objective of this Government to increase expenditure on scientific research to 1.5 per cent of the Gross National Product is several years down the road. In fact, many of the other western industrialized countries, Japan included, are already spending 2.5 per cent of their Gross National Product on scientific research. Is there any Member here who really believes we are spending too much tax money for scientific research? If we are, are we going to leave it to the private sector, which has failed up to now for reasons which I do not have time to discuss today, to attain 1.5 per cent of GNP expenditures for scientific research? If they will, how will we get our expenditures up to 2.5 per cent GNP?
We have had report after report after report about the bad state of our forests. There is a recent one from the Science Council. We had a debate on Tuesday on the whole question of our forest industry. The Science Council made a report a few months ago, the last of many reports made by various research institutes saying we are cutting down our forest at twice the rate they are being replaced. Twenty-five years down the road, unless we take some pretty drastic steps at the federal and provincial Government levels, the forest industries on which several hundred thousand people in Canada depend for a living will no longer be with us. Should we be cutting down on reforestation expenditures?
What about our fisheries? We just had the federal Liberal Government reach agreement with two provincial Conservative Governments, the Government of Nova Scotia and the Government of Newfoundland. They reached a major agreement for the restructuring of the fishing industry in Atlantic Canada which will mean a major expenditure on the part of the federal Government and the Provinces. Why, Mr. Speaker? Because the fishing industry in its free enterprise form simply could not operate on a sound financial basis, for reasons which I do not have the time to discuss, nor am I expert enough to go into detail in any case.
Why did the federal Liberal Government and the two provincial Conservative Governments go into this? Because there are 60,000 or 70,000 people in Atlantic Canada who are totally dependent for a living on the fishing industry. Here you have another example of Government expenditures at the federal and provincial level.
Let us take agriculture as another example. Our agricultural industry is in competition with the agricultural production of

many countries. If we have been able to develop new products, it has been because Government expenditures for agricultural research have resulted in the development of new products, such as earlier maturing grains and so on. Is there a suggestion on the part of the Hon. Member for Capilano that we have been doing too much? I challenge Hon. Members who think that governments are spending too much money or are taking too much out of the Gross National Product-and many of them apparently believe that-to be honest and to indicate how governments can spend less.
1 agree with those people who say that government at every level is not always as efficient as it could or should be. Also I agree with them that, with care and effort, inefficiencies can be eliminated or reduced. However, there is no evidence that savings made in those ways will have a very substantial effect upon the expenditures of governments. As the Hon. Member for Alberta East said a few moments ago, increased government expenditures are not just happening in Canada; they are happening in every country of the western world.
I would like to deal very briefly with another point mentioned by the Hon. Member for Capilano. I believe he said that he felt we had gone too far in government programs which were conceived and directed toward achieving a redistribution of wealth. The statistics do not bear out that argument at all. According to the ones prepared by Statistics Canada, the percentage of the GNP which goes to the bottom 20 per cent of Canadians-that is the 20 per cent of Canadians who have the lowest incomes-has been 4 per cent for 30 years or more. Sometimes it has been 3.9 per cent or 4.1 per cent, but it has been 4 per cent for at least 30 years. The percentage of the GNP which goes to the top 20 per cent-in other words, to the top fifth, high income earners-has been 40 per cent for the last 30 years. Sometimes it is 41 per cent or 39.5 per cent, but it has been around 40 per cent.
1 hope the Hon. Member for Capilano will deal with the point I have made. How can he say that we have gone too far in our programs of redistribution when in fact increases in pension, medicare, hospital care and other good programs which have been implemented, programs supported by all Hon. Members of Parliament, have not changed income distribution in Canada?
In closing, let me indicate that I look forward to the future day when the Hon. Member for Capilano and others who believe, as he does, that governments are doing too much will tell us and the people of Canada just how they expect governments to do less, to spend less or to take a smaller percentage of the GNP than they have taken in recent years.

First, I say to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) that in this fiscal year the country is facing a $31.3 billion deficit. We are spending $31.3 billion more than we are taking in in revenue. The tragedy is that 22 cents or 23 cents out of every dollar of tax by Canadians into

the federal system goes into interest payments on the accumulated debt, which is now approximately $140 billion. I believe it was $134 billion and now it is around $140 billion. If we add the debt the Crown corporation sector is accumulating in borrowings from the private sector, which does not show as a national debt, I think it totals around $165 billion. The 22 cents out of the tax dollar is not on the Crown corporation debt; it is on the debt of the federal Government.
I acknowledge the correctness of what the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North said in that the transfer payments among governments have increased and escalated very severely and that they are delivering transfer payments, in terms of indexing costs, to cover programs such as medicare and all the others of which we are so proud. My point is that the nation will lose all those programs if we do not address some fundamentals.
In terms of addressing transfer payments which take up about two-thirds of our budget, I think we have to conduct a complete analysis of the competing services which the two levels of Government are delivering to the people. I was told by the late Auditor General, James Macdonell, that if we did an inventory of the competition between the federal and provincial Governments, probably in the first year we could address $5 billion of that transfer payment and, over the next three or four years, address another $5 billion. That study has not been done. It is a study that we should conduct because the survival of our system and quality of life depends on it.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to make two short points. First, I suggest to the Hon. Member for Capilano that we have a very large deficit, not because we are inefficient but because we are in a recession. If instead of 11 per cent to 12 per cent unemployment we had unemployment of 5 per cent to 6 per cent, or if we had another 500,000 or 600,000 people working, they would be earning money and paying income taxes instead of drawing unemployment insurance and would be purchasing goods and services on which companies would be paying corporation taxes and sales taxes. Then our deficit would be much smaller than it is.
My second point is one I made before. I had the greatest respect for the former Auditor General, Mr. Macdonell; I sat on that committee for a while. I had great respect for his ability. Many of his suggestions and proposals to the committee and to Parliament were worth while. Some have been implemented, but he was not an expert on the services Canadians need; he was an expert accountant. He was not an expert on medicare, hospital care, unemployment insurance or welfare.
I am doubtful about this $5 billion figure which the Hon. Member for Capilano pulled out of the hat. If the polls are correct, and if in a year or two down the road we have a Conservative Government, he will have an opportunity to show us whether in fact his arguments are correct.
Let me close by saying that of course we are concerned about the deficit. The deficit would not be the problem it is if we were not in a recession and did not have 1.5 to 1.75 million

Mr. Speaker, I just want to follow up on the exchange that we have heard from the two extremes on the other side of the House. I listened to the comments of the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) and was struck by the fact that we always have this blinkered focus on money rather than its use. I would like to put some of his comments into prospective.
First, the deficit we are currently facing is indeed a problem for the federal Government. However, the alternative would be to put an enormous damper on our economy by shrinking that deficit. Second, the deficit represents an investment in the safety net and for the recovery projects that are helping Canadians during a slow economic period and coming out of that period. Third, he should take into account that there are some small or negligible over-all provincial deficits. Our transfers paid their bills. Therefore, we are assuming many of the provincial debts at the federal level. Finally, I would like to point out that this terrible interest burden that he sees is in fact money paid by Canadians to Canadians in the form of interest on that debt, such things as interest on Canada Savings Bonds.

Mr. Speaker, as the NDP Treasury Board critic, I want to put a few comments on the record concerning Bill C-96, an Act to make certain amendments, as the Minister said in his speech on November 19, to enable Treasury Board further to improve financial control and accountability in departments and governments by the Government of Canada. That is a very admirable task. However, I maintain that the improved financial control and accountability being put forward in these amendments, which I just received this morning and have not had an opportunity to consider in depth, is not good enough. I would like to talk about the principle of what is going on.
When looking at improved control and financial accountability, very often those who draft the amendments look only at the efficiency with which government operates. I do not think that is good enough. Many speakers this morning have mentioned J. J. Macdonell, the former Auditor General. I was associated with him through the Public Accounts Committee. I had many very interesting learning experiences through the contributions Mr. Macdonell made to the Public Accounts Committee and, as Auditor General, to the people of Canada.
Mr. Macdonell often stressed that there is a need to look at more than just the efficiency by which government operates.
He referred to the three "E's". You have to look at economy, whether Government is getting the best bang for the buck. Quite often it does not do that. Second, you have to look at efficiency, of course, which the drafters of these amendments so often only look at. Third, you have to look at the effectiveness of what is actually happening to the people if this country through programs being delivered by the Government, Crown corporations and agencies.
The responsibility of the Government and Crown corporations is to deal in terms of our national priorities and responsibilities. If the Government has an over-all responsibility to the people of Canada, there should be some fairness to those at the top end of the economic ladder and those at the bottom. There should be some sense of fairness and equality in the distribution of wealth in this country. That does not now exist as the major responsibility for this Government, many provincial Governments, or possibly anyone who has the control of power in the federal Government today.
I can think of some real abuses of our system and the reason why there is such a need for financial control and accountability. Looking at the three "E's", economy, efficiency and effectiveness, I again go back to my experience in the Public Accounts Committee when I arrived here as a new Member of Parliament. The Committee was dealing with Atomic Energy of Canada and the heavy water plant that had been built at La Prade and never used. It was mothballed at a cost of hundreds of millions of dollars to the taxpayers of this country.
It was also considering the heavy water plants at Glace Bay and Port Hawkesbury. AECL had come to the Public Accounts Committee and the Government of Canada asking for forgiveness of loans of, if memory serves me correctly, $186 million. The Government subsequently forgave these loans to AECL. Beyond that it provided AECL with future budgets to continue the production of heavy water. That was well because it provides jobs for people in Glace Bay and Port Hawkesbury. It is an industry that is complementary to the production of Candu reactors. When you look at that example closely, Mr. Speaker, you find there was not good regard for economy, effectiveness or efficiency. Although heavy water is still being produced at Glace Bay and Port Hawkesbury, we cannot sell any Candu reactors. If we do not sell reactors, we cannot sell the heavy water. Heavy water sales are contingent on the sale of Candu reactors except for a few minuscule gallons used for a topping off process.
Many countries which have purchased reactors from Canada have their own heavy water plants. When we sell a reactor to Romania or some other country, they want to create jobs there. Even if we were successful in selling more Candu reactors, we would still have a problem selling heavy water. Those countries interested in reactors to produce hydroelectric power are interested in having their own heavy water plants.
What is happening is that we are stockpiling heavy water. I again stress the importance of having these jobs for Canadians. However, if you took the budgets of this now useless industry in Canada year after year, plus the $186 million forgiven by the federal Government to AECL, you would find that you

could give to each of those employed in that industry $50,000, $100,000 or $200,000 and also retrain them or let them go into a business of their own in some other area.
The point I am trying to make, Mr. Speaker, is that there is not very much regard for the three E's-economy, efficiency and effectiveness. 1 do not say this in a partisan way, but so often the amendments made by the Government to the Financial Administration Act look only at the efficiency aspect. That is not good enough. We must look at the fairness that exists within the country. We must look at the national debt, and 1 personally think the national debt is a very serious problem in the country.
The national debt has been built up over a number of years. I do not know when the federal Government last had a balanced budget.

Another example of what I have been speaking of is Eldorado Nuclear, a Crown corporation. That Crown corporation is one of those that wants no interference from the Government of Canada or from the Auditor General. One would think that Eldorado Nuclear belonged to the private sector. I maintain that as long as that company is a Crown corporation or a Government department or agency, it has a responsibility to the people of the country to keep in line with the national priorities and objectives of the Government. It must fit into some kind of strategy. The bottom line on the balance sheet cannot be its only motivating factor. If it were, it should go to the private sector.
Eldorado Nuclear does not belong to the private sector, Mr. Speaker, and I would not want to see it belong to the private

sector because of the nature of the industry in which it is involved and the touchy situation that exists over exports of uranium. However, that is an entirely different topic and I will not go into it here today.
There could be another savings for the people of Canada through Eldorado Nuclear, Mr. Speaker. That Crown corporation once ran a uranium mine in the riding I represent at a place called Beaverlodge or, as it is better known to many people, Uranium City. In the year prior to the closing down of Uranium City and the mine at Beaverlodge, Eldorado Nuclear spent in excess of $100 billion. All of a sudden one morning, the people of Uranium City woke up and the news was that Uranium City and the Beaverlodge mine had closed down. When I was first elected to represent that area, that community consisted of over 3,000 people. It declined to a population today of about 250 people because of the "sound planning" of a Crown corporation.
I know that my time is running, short, Mr. Speaker, but I would like to say that in addition to Bill C-96, I would very much urge the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) to bring forward Crown corporation legislation which would make Crown corporations accountable to the people of Canada through Parliament, because today those Crown corporations are seemingly not responsible to anyone. When the Public Accounts Committee would like the Auditor General to do a comprehensive audit on, for instance, Eldorado Nuclear, officials of Eldorado Nuclear say: "No, we do not want to work with you". I maintain that Crown corporations have a responsibility to work with us because we do represent the people of the country. Crown corporations do have a responsibility in carrying out national priorities, objectives and strategies. I think Crown corporation legislation would go a long way toward making those agencies outside of Government departments more accountable to the people of Canada.
Before I was interrupted a few moments ago, I was about to say a few words about the national debt. I believe the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) was correct when he mentioned the figure of about $165 billion as being the amount owed by the Government of Canada. That in effect is our national debt and does take into consideration the money owed by some of the Crown corporations. The figure I have been using is not $165 billion but $166 billion, for which in some way the people of Canada are financially and ultimately responsible.
What about the other side of the ledger? What are the assets?

The assets of the Government of Canada can never be determined. If the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) would pay attention to some of his own committee work, he would know that the Government cannot determine what Canada's assets are because it does not know. One of the reasons it does not know that, Mr. Speaker, is that the Government follows different accounting procedures from anyone else in the country. I have maintained in the House before, Mr. Speaker, that if any farmer, businessman or

Financial Administration Act
individual kept their records and submitted their income tax returns on the basis of that kind of information, they would be sued for income tax evasion.
They would be in jail.

They would be in jail, Mr. Speaker, because no one else in the country can get away with the things with which the federal Government can get away. 1 think that that is shameful. Hon. Members across the way smile and laugh about the financial state of the country.
The late J. J. Macdonell had said on many occasions, as have others in the House, that we have lost control of the public purse. We have lost control of the public purse because we have perpetual deficit financing year after year. Among other things, the NDP has always been accused of being a Party of big spenders. However, I maintain as an individual that it would not matter who came into power. No one could do any worse than the current administration. It is trying to come to grips with the situation through some of the amendments we are dealing with today, and I admire that. However, we in the New Democratic Party believe that we can only use deficit financing when it is an investment in our future for which there will be a return either in terms of financial return or programs for the people of Canada. However, we cannot continually use deficit financing simply for the sake of deficit financing in an attempt to keep all of the voters happy and try to buy people throughout the country with their own money.
That method seems to be working, but it is getting to the point where 1 do not believe the Government of Canada can continue to use deficit financing to the extent it is today. I do not think we need to sacrifice many of the social programs and responsibilities which the Government has a mandate to carry out in order to achieve or at least begin to work toward balanced budgets within the country. The tax base is already there, Mr. Speaker.
1 would like to point out that I was somewhat dismayed by the last budget that came down because of the share the large corporate sector paid in terms of the revenue that is derived by the Government of Canada. Back in the 1950s, the breakdown of the revenue that came to the federal Government was about 50 per cent from corporations and 50 per cent from individuals. That has decreased for the corporate sector over the years. The corporate sector now pays about 13 cents on every dollar, as opposed to 50 cents at one time, to the Government of Canada. There is some imbalance there which I believe needs to be corrected.
The Government of Canada will have to come to a day of reckoning with the people of Canada very soon. I do not think it will find it quite so humorous when the credit rating of this country dwindles in terms of our respect throughout the global community. The only reason we have been able to succeed and to deficit finance for so long, as far as I am personally concerned, is due to the vast resources that we have in this country. If we were like some countries in the world, the
bankers would have stepped in and stopped us a long time ago. The only way there could have been success in this country without the rich resources which we have within our people and our natural resources is by revolution instead of democratically speaking out within the House of Commons and the institutions which this country has to protect democracy.
As I have said, I believe the Government must come to a day of reckoning. I think it would be much better for the Government, whether a Liberal Government or some other Government, to come to the sensible conclusion that it must do something with the financial administration of the country before the people of Canada decide for it through a general election.
1 believe Canadians generally and the Government particularly, through this institution, would be much better off to entrench some power back in Parliament itself. Members of Parliament feel frustrated in the role they must play in dealing with the financial accountability of the Government of Canada. For instance, looking back on the Public Accounts Committee when it forgave the $186 million that the AECL owed the Government of Canada, I know that individual Members of Parliament or even all Members of Parliament in Opposition could not have done anything to stop that from happening if the Government wanted it to go through.
1 think we must look at the role of Members of Parliament so that they can play a meaningful role on behalf of their constituents in examining the public purse, ensuring the maintenance of social programs and the over-all responsibility of providing a better distribution of wealth within the country. I hope that happens very soon.

Mr. Speaker, there have been a number of very interesting comments made during this debate. It is tempting to respond to them at some length. Certainly there should be greater attention given, and perhaps this will be the case, to the very strong espousal by the spokesman for the NDP of an early move to balanced budgets. However, I hope that, perhaps on another occasion, we can explore this very interesting joining of forces with the Official Opposition.
Rather than doing so at this time, I would like to assist the House, since we are going into Committee of the Whole, by presenting to it some comments not only on the Bill itself but on the amendments which have been the subject of intensive discussion on the part of my Parliamentary Secretary and the
November 24, 1983

Opposition spokesmen. In this connection, I want to express my thanks for the courtesy and consideration given by official spokesmen for the Opposition Parties to the amendments which we have indicated we want to present.
I also want to express my thanks for the willingness of the Opposition Parties to facilitate the consideration and passage of this Bill today. Finally, I want to thank my distinguished Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Kitchener (Mr. Lang), for his very effective work with the Opposition spokesmen which has led us to the point where we can confirm that we have had a motion indicating an agreement by all Parties to dispose of this Bill today.
As I said when I spoke to open second reading on November 19, 1982, as a result of comments and suggestions received by the Government, 1 would be proposing a number of changes at the committee stage. These changes would include the deletion of Sections 20.1, dealing with net voting; Section 101, dealing with interdepartmental charging; and Section 102, dealing with the charging and paying of interest. As well, there are a number of technical amendments to the wording.
As I have said, in order to facilitate study of this Bill during Committee of the Whole, I would like to take the opportunity during this stage of debate to summarize some of the provisions of the Bill since it has been a year since this debate opened and 1 presented its basic themes to the House. The principal objective of this Bill is to improve financial controls, accountability and disclosure to Parliament while at the same time streamlining and modernizing certain administrative procedures that have become outdated.
In particular, the Bill establishes in law the fact that only Parliament may forgive a debt recorded on the balance sheet of Canada. It provides a mechanism for the disclosure and approval of loan guarantees by Parliament. It improves accountability for and reporting on the use of appropriations by requiring disclosure in the public accounts of debts incurred but not paid year end. It strengthens controls over the respending of refunds of expenditures by restricting the types of receipts that qualify to be credited through an appropriation and subsequently respent. It provides improved authorities for the recovery of accountable advances and strengthens accountability and liability for losses of public money and public property.
The Bill also contains several changes to the borrowing sections of the Act which were recommended by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). These changes are designed to enable the Minister of Finance and the Department of Finance to approve the administrative process associated with Government borrowing and to respond to changes in market conditions.
In addition, and of particular significance to myself as President of the Treasury Board, are the amendments to Part IV of the Act which formally recognize the role of the President of the Treasury Board with regard to the public accounts and in dealing constructively with any recommendations of the Public Accounts Committee for improving the accounting and reporting practices of the Government.
Financial Administration Act
By way of illustration, 1 want to take a few moments to elaborate briefly on each of these objectives. Subsection 18(1) currently authorizes the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of Treasury Board, to make regulations authorizing deletion from the accounts of debts due to Her Majesty which do not exceed $5,000. Under the deletion of debt regulations, authority to delete debts from the accounts is delegated to the Minister of each department for debts that do not exceed $2,000, and to the Treasury Board on recommendation of the Minister concerned for debts between $2,000 and $5,000.
At present there is no provision for the deletion of debts over $5,000, nor is there uniform criteria for determining when a debt should be considered uncollectable and written off. In addition, action taken to collect debts varies from department to department and there are inconsistencies in the collection of various overpayments as a result of differing authorities in individual Acts.
The proposed changes to Section 18 will provide the Treasury Board with the authority to deal with debts over $5,000 and to prescribe the procedures to be followed and the criteria to be applied when writing off a debt. There will continue to be a requirement in law that debts written off during a fiscal year be reported in the public accounts for that year and, as specified in the proposed Section 18(2), parliamentary authority would be required to write off such debts as loans and investments that are recorded on the balance sheet of Canada.
Section 22 of the Act currently provides the authority to honour loan guarantees but does not provide a mechanism for parliamentary review and approval. We believe that Members of Parliament should have an opportunity to examine and approve each request for a loan guarantee. The proposed amendment to Section 22 will provide a simple mechanism for parliamentary review and approval, and should certainly deal with the concern of Hon. Members of Parliament with regard to the use of letters of comfort.
Several of the proposed amendments are directed at improving disclosure and accountability to Parliament for the use of appropriations. Changes to Section 30 will require that debts owing at the end of a fiscal year under a contractual arrangement, or for work performed, goods received or services rendered, be recorded in the accounts of Canada as a charge against the applicable appropriation, even though payment might not actually be made until the following year. This provision will ensure full disclosure on the public accounts of the complete use of parliamentary appropriations by requiring the recording at year end of both amounts actually paid and amounts owing.
As mentioned earlier, changes to Part IV of the Act, Sections 54, 55 and 56, will make the President of the Treasury Board responsible for tabling the public accounts and will involve the Comptroller General, through the President of the Treasury Board, in establishing in consultation with the Minister of Finance the form and content of the public accounts. Mr. Chairman, our deliberations in the Committee of the Whole will prove that, compared to the information I am now going to provide, I was certainly not providing detailed technical explanations of the Bill when I spoke on second reading. They were very general comments compared to the comments 1 am going to provide in answer to my hon. friend.
First of all, the proposed amendment in the form originally tabled is for the following purpose. Chapter 34 of the Statutes of Canada, 1976-77, the Auditor General Act, provides for the revocation of Part VII of the Financial Administration Act dealing with the Auditor General of Canada, and thus it becomes necessary to define "Auditor General" as referred to in other parts of the Financial Administration Act. The definition included in Clause 2 is to indicate that "Auditor General" means the Auditor General of Canada.
There is a proposed amendment to Clause 2(2), the purpose of which is to change the definition of money paid to Canada for a special purpose. The following wording is substituted:
"money received by Canada for a special purpose" includes all money that is paid to, received or collected by a public officer under or pursuant to a statute, trust, treaty, undertaking or contract, and is to be disbursed for a purpose specified in or pursuant to such statute, trust, treaty, undertaking or contract;
I want to propose an amendment as follows:
That subclause 2(2) of the English version of Bill C-96 be amended by striking out line 26 on page 1 and substituting the following:
"to, or received or collected by a public"
I do not know if you want me to cease speaking now, Mr. Chairman, while you put the amendment, or whether you will permit me to go on and state the object of the amendment. I want to be very scrupulous with respect to procedure. Perhaps I can say that the object of the amendment is to extend the definition of money paid to Canada for a special purpose to include money received or collected by a public officer. The object is to have a technical improvement in wording.
There are other amendments to the Act.
Financial Administration Act

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The Chair would like first of all to dispose of the first amendment proposed by the Minister.
Mr. Chairman, can the Minister give a few examples of how the addition of the word "or" extends the definition?

Mr. Chairman, I am advised that the purpose of the amendment is to indicate that moneys may be received by or paid to a public officer even though he does not formally collect it. For example, a prisoner entering an institution has to place any funds with which he enters the institution into the hands of a public officer who holds it for him during the period of his incarceration. This is an example of the kind of situation this change in wording is intended to address.

1 do not want to belabour this, Mr. Chairman. There has to be a reason for it. Clause 2(2) reads:
"money received by Canada for a special purpose" includes all money that is
paid to, received or collected by a public officer under or pursuant to a
statute-
The amendment adds the word "or" Does that mean moneys received by prison officials from people who are incarcerated can be put into a special account so that it can be paid without interfering with the accounts of Canada? Is that all the word "or" does?

As 1 understand it, funds received by public officers in those circumstances are held in trust by the public officers until the term of imprisonment is over. To repeat what I said before, the amendment is designed to recognize the fact that moneys come into the hands of public officers which are not formally paid to them. They take possession of the money in ways which do not indicate or suggest formal payment. With respect to prisoners, the moneys they bring into prison are shown as liabilities on Canada's balance sheet.
Mr. Chairman, I have to ask again how does the amendment make such a significant difference? The original wording said "paid to, received or collected". My problem is with the language.

Mr. Chairman, the distinguished Opposition spokesman and I share a similar difficulty. I am told the word "or" was added on the advice of legal draftsmen. Advisers to the Department of Justice said it was necessary in order to cover the kinds of situations I outlined. Perhaps had he and I been dealing with this on our own we would not have done this, but we are acting on the advice of counsel in the Department of Justice with respect to the drafting of this Bill.

I am still having difficulty, Mr. Chairman. I do not want to hold the Bill up, but it is just that I am really trying to understand the significance of the change. I do not trust draftsmen of legislation because they can mangle the language I was educated in quicker than anyone else. I get very worried when 1 see an amendment adding the word "or".
I have read this five or six or seven times and tried to understand the significance. Does it make the accounting

November 24, 1983
easier? Does it make it easier to return the goods received from, say, a prisoner by a public officer? Does it avoid an intensive amount of detail in the accounts of Canada? Why has it been amended?

As I understand it, this amendment is not being made for accounting reasons but for legal reasons. That is to say, and 1 am venturing my own view on the matter, technically it could be argued that if this word "or" was not placed in the Act, moneys which public officers took control of in circumstances of the kind 1 outlined, that is to say a prisoner coming into a penal institution and having funds in their possession taken over by public officers, whould not be handled in the same way as moneys paid voluntarily to a public officer. This may be a rather fine point but this is my understanding of the distinction which was not covered in the Act as originally presented and which we are now advised should be dealt with by the addition of the word "or". We are dealing with two sets of circumstances which are definitely different although it may not appear to be that different on the surface.

CALL FOR EXTENSION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION TO CONTINENTAL SHELF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the then Minister of State for Finance, on the 29th of June, 1983, tabled a notice of a Ways and Means Motion to apply the customs and excise jurisdiction of Canada to the Continental Shelf of Canada. He went on to indicate that amendments to legislation affected would be introduced accordingly. This and many other similar motions are even yet left on the table.
Shipbuilding and repair represents a major industry in both the national and the provincial contexts. The federal Government's initiative, after much encouragement by the shipbuilding and repair industry, is consistent with its policy of extending Canada's offshore jurisdiction beyond the current 12 mile territorial limit. The increase in resource exploration and the development on Canada's Continental Shelf beyond that 12 mile limit, a more uniform application of existing rates of duty on shops under the Customs Tariff, and the necessity to introduce a greater degree of equity and fairness into the shipbuilding industry, make the introduction of these amendments an early necessity. CONSEQUENCES OF PROVINCE OF QUEBEC'S INTENTION TO PUBLISH HISTORY BOOK ELIMINATING WORD "CANADA"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few weeks ago, the distinguished French newspaper Le Monde published an article which said that the Quebec Department of Education was planning to publish a textbook on the history of
November 24, 1983

After failing to convince Quebecers in the May 1980 referendum that its option was the right one, and after giving up on Quebec's senior citizens who, according to Mr. Levesque, are an obstacle to Quebec's independence, the Quebec Government now wants to take advantage of the minds of young Quebecers in their formative years. subtopic: WORK OF LIBERAL PARTY REFORM COMMITTEE
WORK OF LIBERAL PARTY REFORM COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of our Party I want to indicate grave concern that the Reform Committee of the Liberal Party has once again delayed its report. A party described by its hard working, party splitting, leadership hunting President as "still in the Mackenzie King era", must move more quickly. The report describes the Liberal Party as "tired, arrogant, self serving, self satisfied, and irrelevant in some parts of the country." Mr. Speaker, that is not new. Canadians have known that for years. What is new is the revelation that there are some parts of the country where they are not that way. There could be as many as six ridings.
Fortunately there is a saviour on the horizon. It is not the Minister of Energy (Mr. Chretien), who is behind one of the curtains looking for delegates. It is not the white knight from Bay Street who quit in 1975. It is not the hapless ex-Minister of Finance whose 1981 budget destroyed the Canadian economy. No, it is the Liberal party President, the shy and retiring Iona, who says:
I've done a great deal of work on my economics knowledge. 1 can hold my own with all of them.
Who could not hold their own with all of them, in a Party that created 12 per cent unemployment, 13 per cent inflation, and 22 per cent interest rates?
In closing, we want to urge the Reform Committee to move quickly so they can continue the dissension in the Liberal Party.

subtopic: FUNDING OF ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT AND REVIEW PROGRAM
FUNDING OF ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT AND REVIEW PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am deeply troubled by an article which appeared in The Citizen concerning the environmental assessment and review process. I was astonished to find out that, as a result of eight internal evaluations of Government Ministries, the Government's plan has been starved for funds and knowingly deprived of effective leadership-in sum, dealt a body blow to its effectiveness.
The plan is supposed to ensure that every federal activity, from $25,000 annual maintenance operations to multi-billion dollar megaprojects, is checked for potential ecological harm. Under two cabinet directives this was to be carried out. We have just discovered that this is not the case. How can the Government, and especially the Ministry of the Environment, go about touting ecological concerns when the Government does not even enforce its own program assessments?

Mr. Speaker, with my experience in agriculture I know the danger of loose hobby farm laws, but surely there is a greater danger in going to the other extreme and beating into the dirt the poorest farmers who are struggling to survive.
Farmers across Canada, especially those who are trying to save their farms by working at other jobs, and those who are trying to build farms by the same method, are being subjected to continued harassment through vicious interpretations of outdated Section 31 of the Income Tax Act by Revenue Canada. I have seen blueberry farmers, livestock producers, cattle ranchers, and every type of farmer across Canada being subjected to persecution.
Many of those who are being audited and having their taxes increased are farmers pure and simple; their entire life is farming. Valiantly they take other employment to get through a hard time, getting up at three o'clock or four o'clock in the morning to do their farm work, and then going to outside jobs, only to return to finish their farming duties. Is it fair that people who cannot afford to fight back be overtaxed to pay the country's deficit brought about through the incompetence of the Government opposite?
The over zealous interpretation of Section 31 virtually destroys the opportunity of many Canadians to start farms. Farming is a tough, unforgiving business. The country needs farmers and the food they produce. The position of Revenue Canada in this matter ignores not only equity but contravenes the rights of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR EARLY INTRODUCTION OF BUDGET
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Statistics Canada has just released its latest index of leading economic indicators. That index supports the growing concern of reputable economists across the country that the current economic recovery is stalling and that it will almost certainly falter in the new year. I would like to ask the Minister this question. Given that employment dropped by 25,000 in October, that the housing construction sector remains appallingly weak, and that retail sales have been falling in real terms since June, is the Government considering very seriously indeed the desirability of an early budget to deal with these growing signs of weakness in the economic recovery?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR EARLY INTRODUCTION OF BUDGET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as 1 have indicated, I am considering bringing down a budget some time between February and June of 1984. I have not as yet decided on a particular time to do so. I am watching the evolution of the economic recovery and will advise in due time as to the advisability of an early budget or a later budget.
So that my hon. friend will not be unduly concerned, I would like to draw his attention to another statement made by Statistics Canada which came out, not yesterday but this morning. That statement does not refer to the leading economic indicators in August but to industrial production in September. It indicated that seasonally adjusted industrial production increased by a very strong 1.8 per cent in September following an upward revised figure of a 1.1 per cent increase in industrial production in August. While Statistics Canada had come up with only a 0.4 per cent increase in August, it revised its figures and arrived at a 1.1 per cent increase, almost a 300 per cent increase in the figure first issued by Statistics Canada.
1 might also point out to the Hon. Member a review of the ten major forecasters which was published very recently in the latest issue of The Financial Post. That review indicates that growth for 1983 was 3 per cent, and growth for 1984 is forecast to be 4.5 per cent by ten major forecasters.
