November 24, 1983
Oral Questions
able to start the debate on the Throne Speech a few weeks from now.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The Minister will know that the major part of the growth in this country this year took place in the first two quarters. Since then, the economy has been stalled. His budget was on April 19 and it accomplished nothing to make this country grow, improve its economy, or to get us out of a recession.
The fact is that the recovery is stalled. What new initiative does the Minister have in mind that would turn the country around and get it growing again? Or is the fact of the matter as set out by Alfred Apps, reported in Maclean's this week, that the Government's advisers say that no amount of new government initiative will do anything. If that is the case, when will he suggest to the Prime Minister that he call an election?

Mr. Speaker, I think the person who is probably the most stalled in this House is the Hon. Member. He is reported as having said that it would take 15 years for the Conservatives to bring some recovery to the economy. We will do that in less time and a lot faster than he would. 1 suspect he was referring to the time it would take them to get back into office.
If the Hon. Member wants to talk about figures, again I would like to refer him to Statistics Canada figures, not for the first two quarters but for September. The figures for the month of September, which is the third quarter of this year, indicate that industrial production went up by 1.8 per cent. That is in a single month, September. The month of August has also been revised upwards by Statistics Canada, to 1.1 per cent from 0.4 per cent. Therefore, the economic recovery, far from faltering, is proceeding very well indeed. All the forecasters foresee that for this year Canada will have a rate of growth that compares very favourably with the rate of growth in the United States, which is the fastest growing economy in the world, along with Canada.

Mr. Speaker, let us talk about some statistics of today. Interest rates today have gone up for the fourth straight week in a row. Let us talk about the cost of money. Every forecaster and economist is saying that we have to get interest rates down. What is happening is that interest rates continue to rise as Governments borrow 75 per cent of the money available in the marketplace. What action does the Government intend to take to get interest rates down and start the economy growing?

Mr. Speaker, I remind my hon. friend that the prime rate in Canada is at the same level as that in the United States at the present time. The
rates for bonds, after 15 years, are lower than they are in the United States. Consumer loans can be obtained presently at a rate equivalent to the rates that were prevalent over the last 25 years. Mortgage rates for consumers, at 10.25 per cent, are as low as they have been for several years. Therefore I would like my hon. friend to look at the facts on the interest rate side and realize that Canadian monetary policy has been the right one.
We have depressed interest rates as much as we could, and in effect the average Canadian is now getting rates, whether on the mortgage side or on the consumer loans side, which compare with rates which have not been in existence for years and years.

this scheme, if he is saying this will not be something which he introduces in the budget in the springtime?

THE CASE OF DONALD MARSHALL-RESPONSIBILITY FOR HELP IN MEETING LEGAL EXPENSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice who has taken a position on behalf of the Government which I can only describe as heartless and mean-spirited with respect to the plight of Donald Marshall, the Mic-Mac Indian from Nova Scotia.
The Minister will know that the Government of Canada, on behalf of all Canadians, signed an international covenant on civil and political rights which provides, among other things, that:
When a person has by a final decision been convicted of a criminal offence and when subsequently his conviction has been reversed or he has been pardoned on the ground that a new or newly discovered fact shows conclusively that there has been a miscarriage of justice, the person who has suffered punishment. .. shall be compensated-
There is a federal responsibility in this matter and the Minister cannot weasel out by attempting to place it on the shoulders of provincial jurisdiction, since he funds provincial legal aid. How can he now deny assistance to Donald Marshall?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: THE CASE OF DONALD MARSHALL-RESPONSIBILITY FOR HELP IN MEETING LEGAL EXPENSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman is surely aware that international agreements, whatever their validity or application, do not change the constitutional and legal situation in our country. We have many examples where the Provinces have given us authority to agree to certain things internationally and the federal Government takes its international obligations, yet within Canada the obligation rests on the Provinces. I take that to be almost too obvious to state, but in this situation it is worth stating.
The Government of Ontario seems to be assuming its responsibilities in similar matters. It is prosecuting studies in this area with great assiduity and I see no reason why other Provinces cannot also assume their responsibilities.

Mr. Speaker, the question 1 asked deals with a sense of compassion. The Minister demonstrates that neither he nor his Government has one iota of compassion with respect to a very tragic situation where a man spent 11 years incarcerated, under a federal law, with respect to an alleged murder. In view of the fact that the Minister indicated his sympathy, which does not cost him or the Government anything, what steps has he taken to manifest that sympathy? Has he at least called the Attorney General of Nova Scotia and used his good offices to make sure there is compensation? Has he offered any amount of money at all in conjunction with the Province of Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, indeed I have spoken to the new Attorney General of Nova Scotia on this matter. 1 tried to use, as the hon. gentleman puts it, my good offices to have the Province assume its responsibilities. The hon. gentleman says this is a federal law, and so it is, as is everything in the criminal law. But as it happens it is enforced by provincial or municipal police, in this case the police of the City of Sydney, Nova Scotia. They fall under the jurisdiction of the Province, and the case was prosecuted by a provincial prosecutor. That should make it clear enough there was no aspect of federal involvement whatsoever in the unfolding of this case.

Mr. Speaker, I can tell my hon. friend what is happening at the present time. There is no crunch. As a matter of fact the banks have surplus funds available for lending. I have already announced steps that we are taking to bring the federal deficit down and to reduce the call on the market by the federal Government, and I hope by provincial Governments also. There is no reason to believe that the problem that my hon. friend is worried about will arise. We can take steps to avoid that problem. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am seeking the floor at this time to respond to a point of order raised on November 17 by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) with respect to Vote 6b of the 1983-84 Supplementary Estimates (B). I am making these comments to assist in the ruling Mr. Speaker will be making on the matter in due course.
I understand that my hon. friend's point of order was based on two contentions. The first was that the Canada Post
Corporation Act contains no legislative authority for the Corporation to do the kind of things listed in Vote 6b. Therefore, he argued that Vote 6b would provide authority not present under existing legislation. Second, he argued that activities listed under Vote 6b would not result in or contribute to the losses of the Canada Post Corporation.
The Canada Post Corporation Act is not exhaustive in citing the things the Corporation may do. Section 5 of the Act authorizes the Corporation to provide products or services which are necessary or incidental to operating a postal service. All the things listed in Vote 6b are necessary or incidental to the activities which are the objects of the corporation. Section 29 of the Canada Post Corporations Act provides for a deficit appropriation item when the Corporation's income is insufficient to meet its expense. Since its inception the Corporation has invoked this provision and is expected to do so in 1983-84. Therefore, any expenditure will contribute to the deficit.
The Corporation could have proceeded with these projects and the costs would have been included in a lump sum appropriation under Section 29. However, the projects reflect Government initiatives in the fields of decentralization, employment and energy conservation and Vote 6b presents a disclosure of the Corporation's contribution toward these goals. Finally, I am told that there have been past instances when Crown corporations have received appropriations for activities under circumstances similar or identical to the present one.
Canada Post Corporation Vote 6c, 1982-83 Supplementary Estimates (C), had the identical vote title as that for the present Vote 6b. It also listed three of the five projects now listed under the present vote. Also Supply and Services Vote 2', 1981-82 Supplementary Estimates (E), provided funds to Canadian Arsenals Limited for the federal building retrofit and conversion initiative (energy conservation). Secretary of State Vote 70, 1978-79 Main Estimates provided funds to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the specific purpose of a host country broadcasting service for the 1978 Commonwealth Games.
On the basis of these arguments, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the item is in fact in order.

Mr. Chairman, Clause 5 deals with remissions. I would like to receive a little information on remissions. How does one go about getting money back from the Government? I will just briefly cite a case where one of my constituents-a new Canadian, incidentally-filed installment payments of $1,000 in each of the quarters in 1975. One of these $1,000 installments was put on his account and then someone in the Department took it off his account and claimed they sent it back to the Mercantile Bank in Calgary. That bank claimed it never had any such letter and the Department apparently cannot find any letter sending the money back to the Mercantile Bank in Calgary.
When the Department took the $1,000 out of this person's account it left him owing just about $1,000 on his income tax. So the Department went to his account and took out $ 1,000. 1 mentioned this earlier today. As soon as my constituent found out about this, he made representations to the Calgary office, which told him it was just a computer mistake and that it would be corrected any time now. But every week he would go down and be told it was just about corrected. Then the Government removed the Department from Calgary to Winnipeg, and the first thing my constituent was told then was that it was destroying its records and closing the case.
It is terrible and inhuman to close the case when that Department knew that $1,000 was missing. All the Department can say now is that its files are destroyed. Why would a Department destroy files when a case is still in difficulties? Would the Minister advise me just how one could go about getting remission in a case like this? Because this is a very inhuman thing to do to new Canadians who came to this country, trusted the Government and now are finding-as one of their neighbours said-that this Government is almost as bad as the government of the country from which they came.
Financial Administration Act
1 know that the Government does not want to steal this money. However, whether someone in the Department mislaid it, whether someone took it, or whether it was returned to the Mercantile Bank in Calgary, what I am saying is that the money was received by the Department of National Revenue, and the Department of National Revenue is therefore responsible for that $1,000, which should either be credited to this person's account or returned to him.

Therefore, in the kind of case my hon. friend is talking about, the Minister of National Revenue would have to make a submission to Treasury Board asking for an Order in Council authorizing the remission. I would be happy to make inquiries of the Minister of National Revenue, if you would like, in regard to the particular case and to assist in having the matter clarified.

Mr. Chairman, can the Minister explain just what is going to happen? There are a lot of remissions from ports and wharves. Are all of these remissions going to be held on record? What will happen as a result of this amendment is that because the Treasury Board will have authority to prescribe the form in which remissions are reported, then with respect to the public accounts themselves as distinct from The Canada Gazette it is itended that we ask each Department to report the total number of remissions and their total value rather than each transaction in excess of $1,000. I am talking here about the public accounts.
What we are trying to do is to have the public accounts deal with this subject in a more select and meaningful way. Of course, details can be obtained under the access to information legislation and, in any event, I am told they will be published weekly in The Canada Gazette.

Mr. Chairman, a word of explanation about Clause 8. The change in question is being made as a result of the Speaker's ruling on legislating through the Estimates. Section 22 of the Financial Administration Act makes reference to the authority of Parliament to authorize loan guarantees. It has been suggested that such authority must be obtained by an "Act of Parliament" other than the appropriation procedure, which should be used only to obtain funds for programs otherwise approved. We are not talking about citizens who are called to account by the Department of National Revenue. That involves another statute and another enforcement procedure. We are talking about public officials responsible for the collection, management or disbursement of public money who are not acting in a lawful manner.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, Subsection 95(1) of the Financial Administration Act authorizes the deduction or set-off of debts due the Crown against any sum of money due or payable by Her Majesty to such persons. It requires, however, that prior to exercising the set-off procedure the Department obtain an opinion from the Department of Justice that the person is indebted to Her Majesty in the specific sum and the authority of the Treasury Board to make set-off by submission to the Board.
November 24, 1983

Prior to April, 1979, an opinion concerning the amount of indebtedness of a person to Her Majesty was always provided by the legal services of the Treasury Board itself, but because of the volume, over 200 submissions per year, this responsibility was centralized with legal officers in the Department. Experience has shown that the majority of set-offs are related to the collection of money pursuant to statutes such as the Income Tax Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Student Loans Act. Because of the statutory nature of such debts the amount of such debts to the Crown, whether caused by default or as the result of overpayments, are not in question and legal opinions concerning them have been based on figures provided by officers of the Department. Consequently, the Department of Justice considers that in the case of statutory debts a legal opinion concerning the amount due is not necessary.
Subsection 95(1) has been in effect since the Financial Administration Act came into existence in 1951. During the period the section has been in effect, a number of court cases challenging the Government's right to set off have resulted in judgments which have upheld that the Government has a common right to make set-offs. Therefore, the Department of Justice considers that the approval of the Treasury Board is superfluous and can be eliminated without detriment. This opinion is based on the judgment in the Federal Court of Appeal which stated that the only purpose of the Treasury Board approval is to provide a mechanism for the set-off of moneys.
As a result, we propose that Section 95(1) be amended to eliminate the necessity of a legal opinion concerning the amount of statutory debts. I would like to note that a legal opinion will continue to be required to establish the amount of a debt relating to non-statutory obligations, for example, contractual obligations to pay the Crown. Also, the amendment would discontinue the requirement to obtain approval of the Treasury Board prior to set-off. Under this proposal, the appropriate Minister will have the authority to require a set-off in the same manner as was recently proposed in the Income Tax Act.

I could say simply that it is consequential on the amendment proposed in Clause 22, but I will go on at greater length. Part XI, Civil Liability and Offences, contains several sections concerning action to be taken when money has not been collected or properly accounted for and offences result in losses to the Crown. Part XII, Miscellaneous, Section 96 in the Act, deals with the public officers' guarantee account which was established as an indemnity fund to compensate for losses arising from any defalcations of public officers. In recent years the wording of the various sections has led to uncertainty as to the action which should be taken and losses incurred. Furthermore, there are precise requirements for taking action and reporting losses where public officers are concerned and while no equivalent requirement exists applying to losses where other persons are concerned. This leads to the latter class of losses being largely ignored in the reporting process. A study into the subject of losses of public money and property has led to the proposal that there should be one comprehensive policy for action to be taken to cover all types of losses, whether caused by public officers or by others, and whether arising for a defalcation or otherwise.
When the Act first became effective in 1952, Section 98 created the public officers' guarantee account and authorized the transfer thereto of the balance remaining in the former Government employees' guarantee fund, which has been in place since 1936, as a means of self-insurance against losses caused by defalcation by public officers. It was funded by premiums levied on and paid from appropriation moneys in respect of all employees handling or managing public moneys. Prior to 1936, it was the practice for Departments to pay premiums on bonds of indemnity which bonded Government employees, the requirement for bonding having been established August 20, 1869. I do not think there is anybody in the House who would recall that. The sums transferred from the former fund to the public officers' guarantee account in 1952 was $657,000.
Section 98 enables the Treasury Board by regulation to levy premiums on Departments to be paid into the account. No such levies have been made during the life of the account. The amount deposited originally plus repayments and restitution made by defalcating officers have been sufficient to meet all claims authorized by the Treasury Board. The lack of any need to levy premiums on Departments over the last 25 years has removed all sense of the account as a bonding mechanism. It has had the effect of reducing the self-insurance aspect virtually to the same self-insurance situation as applies in the case of other losses such as fire losses.

November 24, 1983
Financial Administration Act
We therefore submit the use of the public officers' guarantee account can be dispensed with. Consequent upon the proposal to abolish the use of the public officers' guarantee account it becomes necessary to make provisions for the disposal of any such balance as may remain in the account on the day on which the proposed amendments to the Act become effective. It is proposed that the clause be included in the Bill for a transitional provision to provide for such balance as remains in the public officers' guarantee account on the coming into force of the amended Act and such sums as may be recovered subsequently against payments made previously from the account to be credited to revenue.
I hope this will assist my hon. friend. In essence, the old Clause 98 has been replaced with the new expanded Clause 91(1) which was agreed to under Clause 22.

PUBLIC WORKS-NATIONAL ARTS CENTRE-RESPONSIBILITY FOR STRUCTURAL DEFECTS. (B) REQUEST THAT MINISTER LAUNCH INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the type of responses we get on the Adjournment Debate it would not be of great consequence whether or not the Parliamentary Secretary is here. It is a departmental answer which is mainly a cover-up.
On October 17, 1983, 1 questioned the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc) on the structural problems of the National Arts Centre. He gave me a very incomplete answer in the House and forwarded me a letter which contained other partial information. Therefore I have a series of questions which I should like to direct to the Government or to the Parliamentary Secretary tonight with the hope of receiving some answers concerning what is happening at the National Arts Centre.
29196

November 24, 1983
Adjournment Debate
There are structural problems in the National Arts Centre. Water is leaking into the garage and maintenance shops. The source of the leakage has been found to be through the sidewalk abutting the west side of the Mackenzie King bridge, which in turn forms the roof over the mechanical room. It is leaking because of failure of the waterproofing in the expansion joint in the garage roof. Apparently responsibility for this is that of the City of Ottawa, as well as for the leaky sidewalks. The joint, which is supposed to provide give when the concrete slabs of the garage expand and contract, has been worn by vibration from OC Transpo buses running along Confederation Square. The costs are estimated to be between $285,000 and $300,000 for correction. The bridge and sidewalks are within the jurisdiction of the City of Ottawa, the National Capital Commission and the Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton.
The Minister stated in a letter dated October 26 that it was his intention to consult with the City of Ottawa, the NCC and the Regional Municipality since the problem is in their jurisdiction. However, in an article which appeared in The Citizen in Ottawa on October 18, a Public Works spokesmen, Mr. Tormi Heinmaa, pointed out that the Department of Public Works wanted the Ottawa-Carleton region to pay part of the repair costs but that they were were not very responsive. He went on to indicate:
It's between ourselves and the National Arts Centre to fund the bill.
There seems to be a little confusion here.
The Minister also stated in his letter of October 26 that he planned to consult with the City regarding these necessary repairs. However, according to The Citizen article of October 18, it would seem that some consultation has already taken place and that the City does not seem agreeable to funding part of these costs, as was stated. I am most interested in knowing what part of the costs is being referred to, and if the Minister was aware of the consultation which seems to have already taken place.
Has it been determined as yet who will pay for these repairs? Has the Minister made any formal request to the NCC, City of Ottawa or the Regional Municipality for payment? It was made clear by architect Alexander Topolski in a memo dated Setptember 21, 1983 to the Chief Property Manager of Public Works that if prompt action was not taken, the water penetration would cause further damage. Of course this would mean most extensive repair work and in turn would cost more money. It was further recommended that the repairs should be completed before the onset of freezing temperatures. Has the Minister seen to it that immediate remedial action be taken to ensure the cost of repairs does not expand?
The Public Works spokesman, Tormi Heinmaa, stated as well:
Really, the workmanship in many places around the Arts Centre is not up to very good standard.
I would like the Minister or his Parliamentary Secretary to tell me why the workmanship is not up to standard. Was the
building originally constructed poorly, or has it over the years been allowed to deteriorate? If the latter is the case, why has there not been regular inspections to ensure everything was maintained up to par? If the construction was poor to begin with, I believe there should be an investigation into why the workmanship was below an acceptable level. Further, it should be ascertained as to who will receive the bill for all the necessary repairs.
These are legitimate questions. I hope to receive an answer from the Government tonight as to who allowed all this sloppy workmanship at the National Arts Centre.

subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS-NATIONAL ARTS CENTRE-RESPONSIBILITY FOR STRUCTURAL DEFECTS. (B) REQUEST THAT MINISTER LAUNCH INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few details to what the Hon. Member said in his question on October 17 of this year. First of all, after a period of heavy rain last September, it was found that water was running from the ceiling of the NAC garage into the central stores and the air vents near the mechanical room.
At the request of the NAC, departmental experts immediately proceeded to investigate what caused the leak. They found that water was leaking through the sidewalk abutting the west side of the Mackenzie King bridge, which forms the roof over the NAC mechanical room.
Our Department immediately started with emergency repairs to the waterproofing of the expansion joints of the garage roof located under the sidewalk. I should point out that the entire sidewalk abutting the NAC was built fourteen years ago as part of the Mackenzie King bridge and the west side of the traffic way. Actually, the road was entirely rebuilt over the NAC garage, stores and mechanical room. Over the years, it has been very difficult to find and correct the defects, leaks and damages caused by water penetration. These problems were mainly attributed to causes such as breaks in drain pipes or the road's defective or deteriorating expansion joints and catch basins.
However, during the last two years, bus traffic has increased considerably, and it is suspected that this too has speeded up deterioration of the waterproofing membrane between the road bed and the garage roof, especially near the expansion joints in the ceiling. The sidewalk has also deteriorated as a result of normal exposure to the elements and the fact that it is constantly exposed to potential damage by increasing vehicle traffic. Furthermore, sidewalk blocks are often damaged by snow removal equipment. Together, these factors have helped create the need for maintenance and repairs. To correct the water penetration problems, our Department is now carrying out the emergency repairs I referred to earlier, at an estimated cost of about $80,000. The repairs are part of a more ambitious project now under consideration, to correct problems arising from the condition of the sidewalk along the entire south side of the NAC and the western access route towards Elgin Street, and to the north along the west side of the
November 24, 1983

building as far as the ramp at the northwest corner. Work on this project will start at the point where present repairwork is supposed to finish, which will reduce the total estimated cost by $285,000.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should point out that the NAC is responsible for maintenance and operations in the entire complex, according to the twenty-year lease currently in effect, which expires in May 1989. As the landlord, our Department provides, on demand, any professional and technical services that may be necessary. I can assure the Hon. Member that it would be useless to carry out an independent investigation of the problems at the NAC, since our professional staff, with the help of NAC personnel, is quite capable of resolving any problems that may arise.
Discussions are now taking place with the various authorities involved, namely, the National Art Centre, the National Capital Commission and the Ottawa-Carleton Regional Municipality, regarding the feasibility of sharing responsibility for and costs of these repairs.

subtopic: CUSTOMS AND EXCISE-ESTABLISHMENT OF DUTY-FREE SHOPS IN ONTARIO
CUSTOMS AND EXCISE-ESTABLISHMENT OF DUTY-FREE SHOPS IN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 24 of this year I raised a question about the establishment of duty-free stores in Ontario, page 28260 of Hansard. The Minister's answer was unacceptable. Therefore, I would like to speak to the issue of duty-free shops and the policy of the federal Government toward them.
As the Member for Erie, I represent the Town of Fort Erie, which is one of Canada's largest vehicular points of entry. Despite this fact, I have not received the slightest indication from the Minister that there might sometime be a duty-free shop opened in that town. Indeed, the pilot programs or projects have been located in some rather remote western towns. How they propose to gather data from these out of the way border crossings and make it appear relevant to crossings in Ontario such as Cornwall and Fort Erie, I simply do not know.
Ironically, Ontario seems to offer the most potential for the development of profitable duty-free shops yet, according to the Minister, the Province of Ontario has "chosen to protect its state monopoly and thus thwart private enterprise which the Canadian Government wants to promote through its duty-free shops national program."
1 applaud the Minister's reference to encouragement of private enterprise. Believe me, it is a real surprise to hear that from a Liberal-socialist Cabinet which has nationalized everything from soup to nuts. I refer to its expensive parasitical Crown corporations, from Petro-Canada, with the free seat cushions for Blue Jay fans, to the Canadair fiasco where executives lease aircraft from other companies to Canadair for their own travel, thus lining their own pocketbooks at the taxpayers' expense.
Adjournment Debate
Be that as it may, the Minister and I seem to differ on the role of the Province in the duty-free shop situation. He insists that it is the fault of the Government of Ontario, that the situation seems to be at a stalemate. He is correct in stating that the LCBO is insisting on the right to brand selection, choosing of candidates to manage the outlets, etcetera.
However, the curt nature of his answers to me in the House, at any rate, seem to tell me that he is rather impatient with the whole issue. Perhaps if he sat down with the Ontario Cabinet and worked the thing out reasonably, with a view to achieving some kind of middle ground, more progress could be made.
The Minister's attitude seems to be, to me at any rate, one of stating what he wishes and obtaining carte blanche to proceed directly in that direction. When things do not work out as planned, he turns to us and tells us to go after the provincial Government.
We have been after the provincial Government. The same day the Minister announced to the House that he had not received a favourable answer from the provincial Ministers I received a letter from the Treasurer of Ontario which reads in part as follows:
I can now confirm that Cabinet has agreed, in principle, to allow the duty-free stores at border crossings, and 1 trust, upon completion of a mutually satisfactory arrangement with the federal Government, the first of these stores will be opening in the very near future-
The news then is not all bad despite doom and gloom from the Minister.
I refer you, Mr. Speaker, to an article published in The Ottawa Citizen of October 25, 1983:
A compromise appears near that would allow duty-free shops at some Ontario-United States border crossings, including Cornwall, Prescott, and Lans-downe, about 15 kilometers East of Gananoque.
Consumer Minister Robert Elgie said that he is confident that the debate between Queen's Park and the federal Government can be settled within the next few months.
I am fully aware of the problems involved in obtaining agreement between the federal and provincial Governments on this highly sensitive matter. However, as 1 have mentioned before, I am optimistic that a compromise can be reached as well. 1 wish to emphasize that there must be attention given to those towns with the best potential for success. Fort Erie is one of those towns.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the employment offered by a duty-free shop would be of benefit to the Town of Fort Erie which has one of the highest unemployment rates in the country. Partisan and political considerations must be laid aside in the selection of candidates for these new projects. If they are, all Canadians can benefit from the job creation potential offered by the duty-free shops.

speakeroldname: Mr. Garnet M. Bloomfield (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: CUSTOMS AND EXCISE-ESTABLISHMENT OF DUTY-FREE SHOPS IN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from the inception of the land border duty-free shop program, it has been recognized by the federal Government that close co-operation

November 24, 1983
Adjournment Debate
with provincial liquor licensing authorities would be required. The problem between the federal Government and the Province of Ontario has centered around the Province's desire to protect its monopoly on the distribution and sale of liquor products in the Province. While the program is designed to provide opportunities to the private sector in general and to small business in particular, the position of the Ontario Government so far is that it wishes to operate the liquor sales outlet itself, a situation similar to that in existence at the Toronto International Airport.
Liquor sales form an integral part of a duty-free shop operation. Experience and research to date indicate that up to 60 per cent of total sales may be attributed to these products. The nature of a land border duty-free shop is somewhat different from an airport duty-free shop. In particular, the nature of the land shops has dictated that Customs and Excise take the position that a private-sector operator would need liquor sales to ensure a viable operation, either from the actual sale of liquor or from the spinoff effect of customers who come into the store to purchase liquor products.
Therefore, there is no intention of proceeding with the establishment of land border duty-free shops without provision for liquor sales. Furthermore, the Department remains committed to its original premise that such shops be operated by the private sector.
The Minister has discussed this issue with Dr. Elgie, the Ontario Minister of Consumer and Commercial Relations. Dr. Elgie agreed to study the issue further. There were subsequent meetings between officials which have led to the belief that an agreement can be worked out through further negotiations. The Minister is anxious that the matter be resolved as soon as possible so that the Department can proceed with the program at Ontario borders, including Erie, hopefully around the middle of 1984.
We are encouraged that the Ontario Cabinet has indicated, to certain Hon. Members of this House, agreement in principle with our views. While the Minister has not yet received a formal communique from Dr. Elgie in this regard, our respective officials will work on the numerous small details which are associated with any federal-provincial agreement. We expect an agreement will be prepared early next year in time for national implementation of the duty-free shop program. Translating principles into practice is not always a simple task, but every effort is being made to resolve this issue at as early a date as possible.
